MESOPOTAMIA · A MODERN AUDIBLE REALIZATION

Sammû · nīš tuḫrim

2 retuning moves · initial string 1: 440 Hz · companion strings: octave · sound: plucked

An audible fourths-and-fifths realization, not a recovered ancient performance. Six designated pairs are set to frequency ratios 4/3 or 3/2. Reference pitch, numerical precision, sound colour and the companion-string octave/unison choice are modern settings. The tablets do not record frequencies in hertz or these fractions.

This file includes its fonts, diagram, audio and numerical record. Open it offline, or use your browser’s Print command to save a PDF. External source links need a connection.

Hear the experiment

Before, then after: strings 1 + 5. Each sound is synthetic.

The last change’s overtones

Marks are the sine partials in this synthetic sound. A guide connects partials at exactly the same frequency; it does not establish what the ancient term “clear” meant.

Every retuning step

Step Action Resulting tuning Strings changed String 1 ratio
0 initial išartum — 1/1
1 tighten qablītum 5 1/1
2 tighten nīš tuḫrim 1 + 8 2187/2048

How to read this model

Six pairs of strings are assigned exact 4/3 or 3/2 frequency ratios. The remaining diagnostic pair is left unclear. Each operation changes only the prescribed string (and its companion for strings 1 or 2), making that diagnostic pair clear. The next diagnostic pair then becomes unclear.

Seven moves in one direction return the tuning name but shift every string by 2048/2187 when loosening, or 2187/2048 when tightening. These fractions are consequences of this model, not ratios written on a tablet. No ancient reference pitch, recorded performance, instrument shape, or exact ancient sound colour is claimed.

The two tuning manuscripts from Ur are fragmentary. Combining them with later string-pair evidence is a scholarly reconstruction. In Mirelman’s edition, supplied scribal omissions use ⟨ ⟩ and text restored across a break uses [ ]. For example, the first loosening case has an editorially supplied description of the diagnostic pair; the third is mostly restored.

Sources and provenance

  1. Sam Mirelman · Tuning Procedures in Ancient Iraq (2013)

    Analytical Approaches to World Music 2(2), 43–56. String names: p. 46; two manuscripts and uncertain instrument: pp. 47–48; preserved/restored clauses: pp. 49–52; seven tunings: fig. 5, p. 52; tightening: pp. 53–54.

  2. Jay Rahn · Was Mesopotamian Tuning Diatonic? A Parsimonious Answer (2022)

    Music Theory Online 28.1. DOI 10.30535/mto.28.1.7. Paragraphs 9–16 distinguish physical strings from later pitch concepts and explain the reversible seven-name network; later sections examine assumptions behind an audible reconstruction.

  3. Sam Mirelman & Theo J. H. Krispijn · The Old Babylonian tuning text UET VI/3 899 (2009)

    Iraq 71, 43–52. Edition of the second manuscript. Read with UET VII 74; the two witnesses are separate tablets, not joining fragments of one tablet.

  4. CDLI P347039 · UET VII 74

    Catalogue record for one tuning manuscript from Ur, Old Babylonian period. The British Museum witness discussed by Mirelman is a cast; do not infer the original tablet’s present location from the catalogue’s collection field.

  5. CDLI P254475 · CBS 10996

    Later witness for named string pairs. The catalogue checked on 22 October 2026 assigns Middle Babylonian, approximately 1400–1100 BCE; Mirelman (2013) used an older Neo-Babylonian dating. Combining witnesses is a scholarly reconstruction across time.
